flashcards.q: How does CloudWatch bill custom metrics, and why is this dangerous?
flashcards.a: Per unique time series -- every distinct combination of metric name, namespace, and dimension VALUES is a separate billable metric ($0.30/mo for first 10,000). Dimensions are multiplicative: one metric name with 10,000 distinct dimension values (e.g. userId) becomes 10,000 billable metrics, roughly $3,000/month.

flashcards.q: How do you avoid the CloudWatch high-cardinality trap?
flashcards.a: Keep metric dimensions to low-cardinality, bounded sets (service, environment, route, status class). Route high-cardinality detail (per-user, per-request) to structured logs (EMF or plain JSON), queried on demand via Logs Insights instead of billed per time series every month.

flashcards.q: X-Ray default sampling rate, and its 2026 status?
flashcards.a: Default: first request per second plus 5% of the rest, tunable per service/route. As of February 2026, X-Ray's SDKs and daemon are in maintenance mode -- AWS recommends OpenTelemetry instrumentation for new work.

flashcards.q: CloudTrail management events vs data events -- default and pricing?
flashcards.a: Management events: logged by default, first copy per region free, extra copies ~$2/100,000 events. Data events: NOT enabled by default, billed at $0.10/100,000 events from the very first event, no free tier.

flashcards.q: What's the classic CloudTrail cost trap?
flashcards.a: Enabling data events account-wide/bucket-wide for a compliance requirement with no scoping ('wide open'), sometimes compounded by overlapping multi-region + single-region trails double-logging the same events (the '2nd-copy trap'). Fix: advanced event selectors scoped to specific resources.

flashcards.q: Name the six Well-Architected Framework pillars.
flashcards.a: Operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, sustainability -- run as a structured review via the Well-Architected Tool, producing a prioritized High-Risk Issue list, not a slogan.

flashcards.q: Name the top 5 line items that dominate a real AI/data-heavy AWS bill.
flashcards.a: 1) NAT gateway data processing 2) Cross-AZ data transfer 3) Idle provisioned capacity (SageMaker endpoints, Bedrock model units, oversized Redshift) 4) Unpartitioned/uncompressed Athena or Redshift scans 5) Unscoped CloudTrail data events + high-cardinality CloudWatch metrics.

flashcards.q: Cost Explorer vs Budgets vs Cost Anomaly Detection -- what does each do?
flashcards.a: Cost Explorer: historical/forecast spend analysis, filterable by tag/service/region. Budgets: proactive threshold alerts (commonly 80%/100% of a target). Cost Anomaly Detection: ML-based alerting on spend deviating from a resource's own historical baseline.

flashcards.q: Why must cost allocation tags be applied at resource creation, not retroactively?
flashcards.a: Cost Explorer/Budgets/Anomaly Detection attribution only works from the point a tag is applied forward -- untagged historical spend has no retroactive attribution, so deferring tagging permanently loses that visibility for the deferred period.

flashcards.q: What is Embedded Metric Format (EMF) and does it avoid the cardinality cost problem?
flashcards.a: EMF lets you emit structured JSON log lines that CloudWatch automatically extracts into metrics -- good for high-volume metric emission because log ingestion is cheaper than PutMetricData and doesn't multiply per dimension the way custom metrics do at the emission layer. But whatever dimensions you configure it to EXTRACT into actual metrics are still subject to the same per-unique-time-series billing -- it doesn't remove the cardinality discipline requirement.

flashcards.q: What is 'idle provisioned capacity' as a cost failure mode, and why is it hard to catch with Cost Anomaly Detection?
flashcards.a: Capacity (SageMaker endpoints, Bedrock provisioned throughput, Redshift clusters) sized for peak and left running at trough. Anomaly Detection is tuned to catch deviations from a resource's OWN historical baseline -- steady idle spend doesn't look anomalous against its own history, so catching it requires a utilization-based review (provisioned vs actual usage), not an anomaly alert.

flashcards.q: What are the six cross-pillar Well-Architected design principles?
flashcards.a: Stop guessing capacity, test systems at production scale, automate with experimentation in mind, build for evolutionary architectures, drive decisions using data, and improve through game days.
